title: Connect Two Custom Network NS
markdown:
# Connect Two Custom Network NS

Every namespace lab so far has connected a namespace to the **host** — one end of a veth pair stayed on the host, the other moved inside the namespace. That pattern answers "how does a container talk to its host?" It does not answer a different, equally common question: how do **two containers talk directly to each other**, without routing through the host's own address space at all?

This is the shape of container-to-container networking on a single node — two isolated namespaces, connected by a private link that belongs to neither the host's default network nor either namespace's gateway. This lab builds that link from scratch: a veth pair with **both ends** moved into namespaces, none left on the host.

![alt text](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/poridhiEng/lab-asset/main/Linux%20Labs/Container%20Networking/ns-to-ns/images/ns-to-ns-overview.svg)

By the end of this lab, you will be able to:

- Create two independent network namespaces
- Create a veth pair and move **both** ends into namespaces, with the host kept entirely out of the path
- Address both ends on a shared private subnet
- Prove direct namespace-to-namespace connectivity with `ip netns exec`

## The Scenario: Two Sibling Containers

**cache-ns** and **worker-ns** represent two containers on the same host that need to talk to each other directly — think a worker process talking to a local Redis cache, entirely over a private link the host's own network never sees. Unlike the host-connectivity labs, there is no `veth-host` here at all: both ends of the single veth pair created in this lab belong to a namespace.

| What | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `cache-ns` | First namespace — represents the cache container |
| `worker-ns` | Second namespace — represents the worker container |
| `veth-a` | veth end that will live inside `cache-ns` |
| `veth-b` | veth end that will live inside `worker-ns` |
| `10.60.0.1/24` | `veth-a`'s address, inside `cache-ns` |
| `10.60.0.2/24` | `veth-b`'s address, inside `worker-ns` |

## Part 1: Two Namespaces, One Veth Pair

Create both namespaces first:

```bash
sudo ip netns add cache-ns
sudo ip netns add worker-ns
```

```bash
ip netns list
```

```
worker-ns
cache-ns
```

Both start completely isolated — nothing but a down loopback, no knowledge of each other or of the host's network.

Now create a single veth pair. This step is identical to every other veth pair you've created — the pair doesn't know yet where either end will end up:

```bash
sudo ip link add veth-a type veth peer name veth-b
```

The difference from the host-connectivity labs happens next: **both** ends move into namespaces, rather than one staying on the host.

```bash
sudo ip link set veth-a netns cache-ns
sudo ip link set veth-b netns worker-ns
```

Check the host's own interface list — neither `veth-a` nor `veth-b` should appear there anymore:

```bash
ip link show type veth
```

Empty. The entire veth pair now lives split across two namespaces, invisible to the host's own network stack — exactly like two containers connected by Docker's internal networking, where the host only ever sees the bridge, never the individual container-to-container links.

## Part 2: Bringing the Link Up

Both ends, and both namespaces' loopbacks, need to come up before anything can cross this link:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec cache-ns ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec cache-ns ip link set veth-a up
```

```bash
sudo ip netns exec worker-ns ip link set lo up
sudo ip netns exec worker-ns ip link set veth-b up
```

Verify both ends report `UP, LOWER_UP`:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec cache-ns ip link show veth-a
sudo ip netns exec worker-ns ip link show veth-b
```

> **Note:** a veth pair's two ends are electrically "linked" the moment they're created — but each end still has its own independent administrative state. Bringing up `veth-a` inside `cache-ns` has no effect on whether `veth-b` is up inside `worker-ns`. Both must be explicitly brought up, in their own namespace, just like both ends needed bringing up in the host-connectivity labs.

## Part 3: Addressing Both Ends

Assign each end an address on the same `/24` — there is no gateway here, no third party relaying traffic; the two addresses need only agree on a shared subnet for the kernel's directly-connected route to do the rest:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec cache-ns ip addr add 10.60.0.1/24 dev veth-a
sudo ip netns exec worker-ns ip addr add 10.60.0.2/24 dev veth-b
```

Confirm each namespace sees its own address:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec cache-ns ip addr show veth-a
sudo ip netns exec worker-ns ip addr show veth-b
```

Each `ip addr add` on a point-to-point veth link automatically creates a directly-connected route for `10.60.0.0/24` in that namespace's own routing table — the same auto-route behaviour you've seen in every earlier lab, just now happening independently inside two separate namespaces rather than one namespace and the host.

## Part 4: Proving Direct Connectivity

From `cache-ns`, ping straight across the link into `worker-ns` — no host address, no gateway, involved anywhere in this path:

```bash
sudo ip netns exec cache-ns ping -c 3 10.60.0.2
```

```
PING 10.60.0.2 56(84) bytes of data.
64 bytes from 10.60.0.2: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.010 ms
64 bytes from 10.60.0.2: icmp_seq=2 ttl=64 time=0.020 ms
64 bytes from 10.60.0.2: icmp_seq=3 ttl=64 time=0.030 ms
--- 10.60.0.2 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 3 received, 0% packet loss, time 3ms
```

Three replies confirm the entire path: both veth ends up, both addressed correctly, both namespaces' own routing tables correctly routing `10.60.0.0/24` out their respective veth interface — with the host never once appearing in the picture.

**Why it matters**: this is precisely the primitive container runtimes build on for container-to-container communication on a single node. Docker's default bridge network, Kubernetes' pod-to-pod networking on a node, and any "two sidecar containers share a network" pattern are all, underneath, variations on this same idea — veth pairs (sometimes via an intermediate bridge, which the next lab in this module covers) connecting isolated namespaces directly to each other, independent of the host's own addressing.

## Conclusion

The host-connectivity labs answered "how does a container reach its host?" This lab answers the complementary question: "how do two containers reach *each other*?" — and the answer turns out to need nothing new, just a veth pair used differently: both ends inside namespaces instead of one end staying on the host.

- A single `ip link add ... type veth peer name ...` pair can connect any two network stacks — host-to-namespace, or namespace-to-namespace
- Each end's up/down state and addressing is independent — always configure both sides explicitly
- Direct namespace-to-namespace connectivity needs no routing table entries beyond the automatic directly-connected route each `ip addr add` creates
- This is the exact building block the next lab extends from two namespaces to three or more, using a Linux bridge instead of a single point-to-point veth pair
